newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Sanctions continue against Libya after U.N. review.
newsitem.headline: Sanctions continue against Libya after U.N. review.

text.p: The Security Council, after a periodic review, on Friday left unchanged sanctions imposed on Libya in connection with the 1988 airliner bombing over Lockerbie, Scotland, council members said.

The sanctions, which include an air embargo, a ban on arms sales and the downgrading of diplomatic relations, were first imposed in 1992 because of Libya's refusal to extradite two men accused of planting a bomb aboard Pan Am flight 103, which exploded over the Scottish town, killing 270 people.

The sanctions, reviewed by the council every 120 days, also penalise Libya for not cooperating in the investigation into the 1989 bombing of France's UTA flight 772 over Niger, which killed all 171 aboard.

Because of Tripoli's non-compliance, the council imposed additional sanctions in 1993, including a freeze on some of Libya's assets abroad and a ban on the import of equipment for oil terminals and refineries. But they do not affect the export of oil or the purchase of oil drilling equipment.

The two Lockerbie suspects, alleged intelligence agents Abdel Baset Ali Mohamed al-Meghrahi and Al-Amin Khalifa Fhimah, have been indicted in Britain and the United States, which demand they stand trial in a Scottish or U.S. court.

London and Washington have rejected offers by Libya, backed by the Arab League, the Organisation of African Unity and the non-aligned movement, for them to be tried by a Scottish judge under Scottish law but at the seat of the World Court at The Hague. Libya says they could not get a fair trial in Britain or the United States.
